Second, parity matters. We regulate obscenity because some expressions corrode the public sphere and harm the vulnerable. Blasphemous derision functions similarly: it corrodes shared moral reference points and invites hostility against believers. If we can restrict lies that ruin reputations or harassment that poisons workplaces, we can restrain publicly disseminated insults aimed at Christian beliefs that poison civic life.

Third, religious liberty includes freedom from sustained, hostile public desecration. A Rhetorical Argument

I. The Historical Argument: Blasphemy Law Is American Law

The notion that blasphemy laws are foreign imports, alien to the American tradition, is historically illiterate. At the time of the Constitution's ratification, virtually every state maintained blasphemy statutes. Massachusetts prosecuted blasphemy cases into the twentieth century. Even the most heterodox founders — Franklin, Adams, Jefferson — consistently argued that republican self-government depended on a moral citizenry, and that Christianity provided the indispensable substrate for public morality.

The answer should be self-evident. Christianity is not merely one lifestyle option among many in the American marketplace of ideas. In favor of enacting blasphemy laws in the United States to protect Christianity, there is a strong, clear, and necessary case to be made. Such laws would not be a radical departure from American values, but a restoration of them.

1. Christianity is the Foundation of the American Social Order and Deserves Special Legal Protection

The United States was not founded as a secular void. It was founded by Christians, upon Christian moral principles, with Christian institutions serving as the backbone of American law, education, charity, and civil society. The Declaration of Independence appeals to a Creator, our laws against murder, theft, and perjury come directly from the Ten Commandments, and for over 200 years, Christian morality was the accepted common ground of public life.

When that foundation is allowed to be publicly mocked, insulted, and degraded without consequence, the entire social order built upon it is weakened. A society cannot long survive if it permits unlimited public contempt for the very faith that gives it its moral coherence. Protecting Christianity is not favoritism; it is self-preservation for the nation.

2. Freedom of Speech Does Not Mean Freedom to Desecrate

The First Amendment was never intended to be a suicide pact. It was intended to protect political debate, not to protect calculated, malicious insult directed at the sacred beliefs of the vast majority of Americans.

We already recognize that freedom of speech has limits. Defamation, obscenity, fighting words, and incitement are not protected. We have hate crime laws that provide enhanced penalties for offenses motivated by bias against religion. If the law can recognize that targeting someone for their religion causes a unique social harm, it can and should recognize that willfully and publicly desecrating the central religion of the country causes a far broader social harm.

Blasphemy laws would not prohibit private disbelief, theological debate, or academic discussion of Christianity. What they would prohibit is the public, deliberate, and severe act of insulting, mocking, or degrading Christian beliefs, figures like Jesus Christ, sacred texts like the Bible, and sacred rites and institutions. There is a clear difference between disagreement and desecration, and the law is perfectly capable of drawing that line.

3. Blasphemy Laws Promote Public Order and True Pluralism

Unchecked public blasphemy breeds division, provocation, and even violence. When activists invade churches to stage profane protests, when artists receive public funding to create work that depicts Christ in filth, when entertainers and corporations profit from mocking Christians as bigoted and foolish, it sends a message to millions of believers that they are despised in their own country.

This constant provocation alienates Christians from public life and creates deep cultural resentment and instability. Blasphemy laws would serve as a necessary cooling mechanism — a legal standard of mutual respect. If we tell citizens they must be respectful of other identities and beliefs in public, it is only consistent and just that the majority faith receive the same, and indeed greater, respect.

4. There is Strong Historical and Legal Precedent

Blasphemy laws are not foreign to America; they are part of our legal heritage. Many of the original colonies had blasphemy statutes. States continued to have them on the books well into the 20th century. The Supreme Court in Chaplinsky v. New Hampshire and other early cases acknowledged that blasphemy and profanity could be restricted as part of maintaining public order.

Nearly every other major civilization in history, including our closest allies like England, Ireland, Poland, and Italy, has had or currently has laws against blasphemy or religious insult. The recent experiment of allowing absolute, unbridled public mockery of Christianity is the historical anomaly, not the rule.

Conclusion: It is Time to Restore Respect

Enacting federal and state blasphemy laws that criminalize severe public insults, mockery, and derision of Christian beliefs, figures, and institutions would be a just and necessary step. Such laws would:

  • Affirm that America honors its Christian heritage;
  • Protect the dignity and religious freedom of over 200 million Christian Americans from targeted public harassment;
  • Restore a baseline of decency and respect to our public square;
  • And strengthen social cohesion by prohibiting acts designed only to offend and divide.

A penalty - whether a fine, community service, or in cases of repeated or aggravated public desecration, imprisonment - would deter those who would treat Christianity as a punching bag.

We protect what we value. If the United States values its moral foundation, its cultural unity, and its Christian people, it must be willing to put that value into law.
